passages.text: Microfabrication of Gelatin Methacrylate/Hydroxyapatite Composites by Utilizing Alternate Soaking Process

To construct a complex three-dimensional (3D) structure mimicking bone microstructure, hydrogel models of polymerized gelatin methacrylate (pGelMA) were fabricated by using stereolithography and modified with hydroxyapatite (HAp) via an alternate soaking process (ASP) using a solution of calcium and phosphate ions. Fabricated pGelMA line models whose widths were designed as 100, 300, and 600 mum were modified with HAp by ASP by changing the immersion time and number of cycles. After ASP, all of the line models with widths of 100, 300, and 600 mum were successfully modified with HAp, and large amounts of HAp were covered with the fabricated models by increasing both the immersion time and the number of cycles in ASP. HAp was observed near the surface of the line model with a width of 600 mum after ASP at an immersion time of 10 s, while the entire model was modified with HAp using ASPs for longer immersion times. The adhesion and spread of mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) on the pGelMA-HAp discs depended on the ASP conditions. Moreover, the HAp modification of 3D pyramid models without alteration of the microstructure was also conducted. This two-step fabrication method of first fabricating frameworks of hydrogel models by stereolithography and subsequently modifying the fabricated models with HAp will lead to the development of 3D cell culture systems to support bone grafts or to create biological niches, such as artificial bone marrow.
Introduction

Bone is a hybrid material composed of organic and inorganic substances, mainly collagen fibers and hydroxyapatite (HAp), respectively. Mineralized collagen fibers assemble and form a hierarchical structure, providing excellent mechanical strength and toughness in cortical bone. Microstructures found in the bone marrow, known as the bone marrow niche, can function as regulators of the maintenance and expansion of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), which can differentiate into all blood cell lineages, including both white and red blood cells. HSCs mainly reside in the bone marrow of adults, and their functions are supported by the bone marrow niche, which contains several types of cells, such as mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), osteoblasts, and endothelial cells. Direct interactions with these cells and indirect interactions through cytokines and growth factors secreted by these cells are important for maintaining HSCs in the bone marrow niche. However, the detailed mechanism by which the bone marrow niche is responsible for maintaining HSCs remains unclear. Although HSC transplantation is a potential strategy for treating leukemia, lymphoma, and immune diseases, it is difficult for HSCs to expand outside of the body. Creating a transplantation model that mimics the bone marrow environment could resolve these difficulties, allowing HSCs to be maintained and proliferated in vitro while maintaining their functions and preparing a large number of transplantable HSCs. Additionally, a model that mimics the bone marrow environment can be used to clarify the mechanism of HSC maintenance in bone marrow in vivo.

Biomaterials based on HAp that mimic bone microstructure have been developed.- HAp is a ceramic that is biocompatible and osteoconductive, and HAp-coated surfaces promote the osteogenesis of human mesenchymal stem cells (hMSCs). HAp-coated hydrogels have been used as bone substitutes in vivo to bind defective bone by implantation. These findings indicate that HAp-coated materials can create a biological environment that enhances cellular function and exhibits a high affinity for bone. To construct bone microstructure mimicking a biological environment, microfabrication techniques have been developed to obtain three-dimensional (3D) models with HAp. One technique is the extrusion method, and the other is stereolithography. In the extrusion method, a resin solution dispersed with HAp was extruded from the nozzle to create a 3D model with HAp. The extrusion method is useful for materials that are difficult for light to pass through, and it is possible to fabricate models with large areas. However, in this method, the print resolution is not as high because the resolution is highly dependent on the nozzle diameter. Stereolithography is based on photopolymerization of a photocurable resin solution. Stereolithography techniques such as laser scanning stereolithography (SLA) and projection stereolithography (DLP) can create more complicated models with structures more precise than those of the extrusion method. Various hydrogel models of photocurable polymers, usually functionalized by introducing acrylate or methacrylate groups, have been fabricated using stereolithography. Although DLP is suitable for the fabrication of large-scale models in a short time owing to two-dimensional exposure using digital mirror device (DMD), the resolution is less than that of SLA. This is because the focused laser spot used in SLA is smaller than the minimum pixel size of DMD. Therefore, it is expected that high-definition reproduction models of bones can be obtained by SLA.

For fabricating bone scaffolds, stereolithography with photocurable ceramic slurry has been reported.- When modeling using a slurry, it is difficult to completely cover the surface of the fabricated models with ceramics and to fabricate complicated 3D models such as lattices. Although degreasing and sintering have been carried out to remove a photocurable resin, there are some problems, such as shrinkage in the fabricated models or in the crystallinity of ceramics. Therefore, we proposed a fabrication method to initially construct frameworks of hydrogel models by SLA and subsequently modify the models with HAp in an alternative soaking process (ASP) method commonly applied for bulk hydrogels. ASP was developed to modify organic materials with HAp. In this method, the polymer surface or hydrogel can be easily modified with HAp after alternately immersing the material into solutions containing Ca2+ and PO43-, and the modified surface shows enhanced bioactivity. The ASP conditions required to form HAp can be controlled by varying the number of solutions exchanged (cycle number, n) and the time in solution (immersion time, t). HAp modification with ASP has been conducted on various types of hydrogels, such as poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA), chitosan (CHI), and gelatin.

In this study, HAp-modified microsized models were created using stereolithography of polymerized gelatin methacrylate (pGelMA), a biocompatible cross-linkable polymer used for bioprinting. Line-shaped models were designed and fabricated as simple models, and a pyramidal model with a complex structure was fabricated to demonstrate modification of the fabricated models with HAp without alteration of the microstructure created by stereolithography. Line-shaped models of various sizes were modified with HAp using the ASP method under various conditions by changing the immersion time and number of ASP cycles. The obtained pGelMA-HAp composite line models were analyzed, and the mechanism of HAp formation by ASP in the pGelMA hydrogels was investigated.
Materials and Methods
Reagents

All reagents were purchased and used without further purification. Gelatin was purchased from FUJIFILM WAKO Pure Chemical Industries Ltd. (Osaka, Japan). Deuterium oxide and lithium phenyl-2,4,6-trimethylbenzoylphosphinate (LAP) and synthetic HAp were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO). Methacrylic anhydride and Acid Yellow 3 were purchased from Tokyo Chemical Industry Co., Ltd. (Tokyo, Japan). Dulbecco's phosphate-buffered saline (D-PBS), calcium chloride, and dipotassium hydrogen phosphate trihydrate were purchased from Nacalai Tesque, Inc. (Kyoto, Japan). Ultrapure water (18.2 MOmega cm) was prepared by using Direct-Q UV5 (Merck Millipore, Burlington, MA). Dialysis tubes (M-25, MWCO = 12 -14 kDa) were purchased from Kenis, Ltd. (Osaka, Japan).
Cell Culture

UE7T-13 cells (immortalized human bone marrow-derived MSCs, Japanese Collection of Research Bioresources (JCRB), Cell Bank, National Institute of Biomedical Innovation, Tokyo, Japan) were cultured in Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium (D-MEM, Nacalai Tesque, Inc.) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA) and 1% penicillin (100 U/mL)/streptomycin (100 mug/mL) solution (Nacalai Tesque, Inc.).
Preparation of Gelatin Methacrylate (GelMA)

GelMA was synthesized according to a previously reported method, with some modifications. Briefly, gelatin was dissolved in D-PBS (10%w/v) at 50  C, and methacrylic anhydride (20%v/v) was added dropwise to the gelatin solution under stirring. After 1 h, the reaction mixture was diluted 2 times with ultrapure water and dialyzed against ultrapure water using a 12-14 kDa cutoff dialysis tube for 4 days at 50  C. After dialysis, the solution was filtrated with paper and then through a polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) syringe filter (pore size 0.22 mum, Merck Millipore, Burlington, MA). After filtration, the solution was lyophilized (FDU-1200, TOKYO Kiki Co., Ltd., Tokyo, Japan). The degree of methacrylation (DM) was determined from 1H NMR spectra recorded using an NMR spectrometer (ECA-500, JEOL Ltd., Tokyo, Japan), following previously published methods. By using the peak of phenylalanine (7.1-7.3 ppm), which was constant before and after the reaction, as a reference, the signals of methylene corresponding to the lysine residue of gelatin and the product were integrated. The DM was calculated using the following formula
Stereolithography

GelMA was dissolved into D-PBS (20%w/v) by heating at 37  C, and LAP (0.5%w/v) and Acid Yellow 3 (0.1%w/v) as a photoinitiator and blue light absorber, respectively, were added to the GelMA solution. We developed several types of stereolithography systems such as the bottom-up method using single-photon polymerization with a blue laser and the direct-write method using a femtosecond laser. In this work, 3D models (plane, line, and pyramid models) were fabricated on glass plates by a laboratory-made SLA system based on a bottom-up method using single-photon polymerization with a blue laser (Cobolt 06-MLD, Cobolt, Solna, Stockholms Lan, Sweden) and ftheta lens (SCANCUBE III 14, SCANLAB GmbH, Puchheim, Germany).Figure 1a shows a schematic of the laboratory-made stereolithography system. The light from the blue laser was turned on and off using an automatic mechanical shutter, and the light intensity was adjusted using a variable neutral density (ND) filter. The laser beam was then collimated to a beam 10 times larger in diameter using a beam expander. Light passing through a beam splitter was incident on a galvanometer mirror (SCANCUBE III 14, SCANLAB GmbH, Puchheim, Germany) and focused on the boundary surface between the GelMA solution and PDMS-coated glass using an ftheta lens. The ftheta lens was designed to scan a flat image plane with an area of 60 x 60 mm2. When the 3D printing process was started, the laser beam was focused by observing the reflected light from the interface between the PDMS and the GelMA solution with a charge-coupled device (CCD) camera and adjusting the focus position of the laser beam. The line models were designed with line widths of 100, 300, and 600 mum. Plane models (ca. 1 cm x 1 cm) with a similar height as line models of 600 mum (ca. 450 mum) were fabricated. A model of a pyramidal structure consisting of three layers, as shown in Figure 1b-d, was fabricated using the same procedure as for the line models. Those 3D-CAD model data were prepared using lab-made software to produce a 3D model. The laser power was 20 mW for the line and plane models and 3 mW for the pyramid models. The laser output values when passing through the variable ND filter in our setup are shown. The layer pitch, hatching distance, and scan speed were 50, 3 mum, and 3000 mum/s, respectively.

Schematic of the laser scanning stereolithography system using a blue laser and ftheta lens (a). 3D-CAD model of the pyramid model of pGelMA hydrogel, bird's eye view (b), top view (c), and side view (d).
Preparation of pGelMA Hydrogel Disc

GelMA was dissolved in D-PBS (20% w/v) by heating at 37  C, and LAP as a photoinitiator was added to the GelMA solution (0.5% w/v). The mixed solution was injected between two glass slides using a spacer (1 mm) to obtain a hydrogel sheet (thickness = 1 mm). Photopolymerization was induced by ultraviolet (UV)-irradiation to the mixture for 10 min with a hand-held UV lamp (SLM-8, wavelength: 365 nm, 1407 muWcm-2, AS One Co., Osaka, Japan). The formed gel sheet was punched into a round shape with a punch (Phi14 mm).
Alternate Soaking Process (ASP) of pGelMA Hydrogel Models

Inorganic modification of the pGelMA hydrogel models was performed using an ASP, as described previously, with some modifications. The fabricated pGelMA hydrogel models or hydrogel discs were immersed in a 500 mM CaCl2 aqueous solution for the indicated times. After the gels were washed with ultrapure water for 10 s, they were immersed in a 300 mM K2HPO4 aqueous solution for the indicated times. The gels were then washed with ultrapure water for 10 s. This process was repeated several times. The immersion time (t) was 10 or 110 s, and the repetition number (n) of the ASP was 5 or 15 cycles. After ASP treatment, the treated gels were washed with ultrapure water and preserved in D-PBS at 4  C before use.
Characterization

The fabricated objects were observed before and after ASP treatment using a VHX6000 microscope (Keyence Corp., Osaka, Japan). After ASP, the pGelMA hydrogels were cut with a scalpel to expose their cross sections. After ASP treatment, the fabricated object was stained with a 1% alizarin red S aqueous solution (pH 6.4) for 1 min and washed in ultrapure water overnight.

The morphologies of modified hydrogels after freeze-drying were observed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM, SU8010; Hitachi High-Tech Corp., Tokyo, Japan), employing an acceleration voltage of 4.0-10.0 kV, and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) mappings were recorded by SU8010 equipped with Esprit 1.9 (Bruker Nano GmbH, Berlin, Germany). Prior to the analysis, the samples were coated with Pd/Pt by using an MSP-1S magnetron sputter coater (Vacuum Device Co., Ibaraki, Japan). Fourier-transform infrared (FT-IR) spectra of the freeze-dried hydrogels after ASP were obtained by using the KBr method (FT-IR 6200, JASCO Corp., Tokyo, Japan). X-ray diffraction (XRD) was performed using a SmartLab II instrument (Rigaku Corp., Tokyo, Japan) with Cu Kalpha radiation (tube voltage: 40 kV; tube current: 45 mA; step width: 0.02 ). After modification, the hydrogel surfaces were characterized using a Raman microscope (inVia reflex, Renishaw Plc., Wotton-under-Edge, U.K.) with an excitation wavelength of 785 nm. Differential thermal analysis (DTA) and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) were performed using a thermogravimetric analyzer (DTG-60A, Shimadzu Corp., Kyoto, Japan). Freeze-dried hydrogels after ASP were placed in aluminum pans and weighed by TGA from 25 to 600  C at a temperature increase rate of 10  C/min. The moisture content was determined by the change in total weight from 25  C to the temperature at which the DTA became zero (ca. 200  C). The mineral content was determined from the residue at 600  C, and the organic content was calculated from the difference in weight change at 200 and 600  C.
Culture of MSCs on the pGelMA Hydrogels

pGelMA hydrogel discs (Phi14 mm) after ASP were immersed into D-PBS for 24 h to remove the residual initiator. Before seeding the cells, the models were sterilized by UV irradiation (254 nm, 4.9 W, 10 min) for 5 min. MSCs were seeded at 1 x 105 cells/well on the prepared models in a 24-well plate (VIOLAMO, AS ONE Corp., Osaka, Japan) and cultured for 24 h at 37  C under a humidified 5% CO2 atmosphere. The cytotoxicity of the models was determined using a live/dead assay, cell viability, and cytotoxicity assay kit (Funakoshi Co., Ltd., Tokyo, Japan) according to the manufacturer's protocol. After 24 h of cell culture, the cells were rinsed 3 times with D-PBS. Calcein acetoxymethyl (calcein AM, green fluorescence; live cells) and ethidium homodimer-1 (EthD-1, red fluorescence; dead cells) were diluted 1:500 in D-PBS. The diluted solution was poured into each well, and the stained cells were washed twice with D-PBS and observed using a fluorescence microscope (X83, Olympus Corp., Tokyo, Japan).

passages.text: Culture of MSCs on the pGelMA Hydrogel Pyramid Model after ASP

MSCs were seeded at 1 x 105 cells/well on the fabricated pGelMA hydrogel pyramid model after ASP at 10 s, 5 c in a 24-well plate, and cultured at 37  C under a humidified 5% CO2 atmosphere. After culturing, the culture medium was removed, and the hydrogels were washed with D-PBS and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde. After washing with water, the hydrogel model was permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100. After being washed with D-PBS, the specimens were stained with 100 nM rhodamine-phalloidin (Fujifilm Wako Pure Chemical Industries, Ltd., Osaka, Japan) for 40 min in the dark. After washing 3 times with D-PBS, the hydrogels were stained with 4',6-diamidino-2-phenylindole, dihydrochloride (Dojindo Laboratories, Kumamoto, Japan) diluted 1:500 in D-PBS for 5 min in the dark. After washing with D-PBS, the hydrogels were observed by using a confocal laser scanning microscope (CLSM) (FV3000, EVIDENT, Tokyo, Japan).
Statistical Analysis

All data are presented as the mean standard deviation (SD). The significant difference between the two samples was determined by Student's t-test in Microsoft Excel for Microsoft 365 MSO. Differences with p-values below 0.05 and 0.01 were considered statistically significant.
Results
Fabrication of pGelMA Hydrogel Models and Inorganic Modification with ASP

pGelMA hydrogel models were prepared by photopolymerization of the hydrogel precursor solution using blue laser stereolithography (Figure 1a). First, pGelMA line models with different line widths (100, 300, and 600 mum, Figure 2a-d) and pGelMA plane models (Figure 2e) were designed and fabricated. pGelMA hydrogel discs were also prepared (Figure 2f). ASP was performed on each model to modify the fabricated pGelMA models with inorganic compounds. ASP was conducted by changing the conditions, such as the immersion time (t) at 10 or 110 s and the number of ASP cycles (n) at 5 cycles (5 c) or 15 cycles (15 c). Microscopic images of pGelMA line models with a 600 mum width before and after ASP are shown in Figure 3a-h. Under relatively mild conditions (such as (t, n) = 10 s, 5 c), a thin layer of white deposit was observed near the surface of the model (Figure 3e). When the soaking time was increased to 110 s, a white deposit was observed in the center of the model; therefore, the entire model was modified (Figure 3g). However, with an increase in the number of cycles to 15, large amounts of white deposits were excessively mineralized to cover the line models (Figure 3f). In the case of 110 s and 15 c, line models were covered with large amounts of white deposits, as was also observed for the case of 10 s and 15 c (Figure 3h).

Optical microscopic and macroscopic images of models of pGelMA hydrogels. The microscopic upper view of line models (scale bar: 1 mm) (a); arrowheads indicate line models of 100, 300, and 600 mum from left to right; the microscopic side view of line models of 100 (b), 300 (c), and 600 mum (d) (scale bars: 100 mum); the microscopic upper view of the plane model (e) (scale bar: 2 mm); and the macroscopic image of the gel disc (f) (scale bar: 2 mm).

Optical microscopic cross-sectional images of nonstained (a-h) and alizarin red S-stained (i-l) line models of pGelMA hydrogels with 600 mum width before (a-d) and after (e-h) ASP at the conditions of 10 s, 5 c (a, e, i), 10 s, 15 c (b, f, j), 110 s, 5 c (c, g, k), and 110 s, 15 c (d, h, l). Scale bars: 200 mum.

Next, the pGelMA line models were stained with alizarin red S (Figure 3i-l). For the models treated with a short immersion time (10 s, 5 c and 10 s, 15 c), near the surface of the line models were stained red, and the centers of the models were not significantly stained (Figure 3i,j). In contrast, for the models treated with longer immersion times (110 s, 5 c and 110 s, 15 c), the whole models were stained red (Figure 3k,l). The distribution of calcium and phosphorus atoms in the cross section of the pGelMA line models after ASP was visualized by EDX mapping (Figure 4a-l). In the samples subjected to ASP with a soaking time of 10 s (10 s, 5 c and 10 s, 15 c), calcium (red) and phosphorus (blue) were detected only in the area near the surface of the line models (Figure 4a-f). In the samples soaked for 110 s (110 s, 5 c, and 110 s, 15 c), calcium and phosphorus were observed both inside and outside the model (Figure 4g-l). From SEM images (Figure 5a-l), plate- and needle-like structures were observed in all samples.

SEM images (a, d, g, j) and EDX mapping of calcium (b, e, h, k) and phosphorus (c, f, i, l) of the cross section of pGelMA line models with a 600 mum width after ASP at conditions of 10 s, 5 c (a-c); 10 s, 15 c (d-f); 110 s, 5 c (g-i); and 110 s, 15 c (j-l). Scale bars: 300 mum.

SEM images of the surface of pGelMA line models with 100 (a, d, g, j), 300 (b, e, h, k), and 600 mum (c, f, i, l) widths after ASP at conditions of 10 s, 5 c (a-c); 10 s, 15 c (d-f); 110 s, 5 c (g-i); and 110 s, 15 c (j-l). Scale bars: 3 mum.
Characterization of the Fabricated Models after ASP

To characterize the inorganic compounds generated after ASP under different ASP conditions, plane models (Figure 2e) were fabricated because a large number of composites were required for FT-IR, Raman, XRD, and TDA/DTA measurements. ASP was conducted on the pGelMA plane models by using the same procedure and conditions as those used for the line models. The FT-IR spectra of the pGelMA plane models obtained after ASP under four different conditions are shown in Figure 6a-d. All of the spectra showed peaks derived from the pGelMA xerogel (Figure 6e). Weak peaks at 1320 cm-1 corresponded to the bending of CH (CH3 group) in GelMA, and broad peaks at approximately 3200 cm-1 corresponded to the stretching of the hydrogen-bonded hydroxyl group (OH) and stretching of amide bonds of N-H. In all samples, significant peaks assignable to the bending vibrations of phosphate groups (PO43-) were detected in the range of 650-500 cm-1 and there was no significant difference in the shape of the peaks. In the XRD measurements (Figure 7a-d), all of the samples after ASP showed strong peaks corresponding to the (002) plane at 26 ; (211), (112), (300) at 32 ; and (213) at 49  from HAp (Figure 7e). The peaks detected in the samples prepared with soaking times of 110 s (110 s, 5 c, and 110 s, 15 c) were sharper than those with soaking times of 10 s (10 s, 5 c, and 10 s 15 c). In addition, peaks corresponding to (020) at 12  and (12-1) at 21  from dicalcium phosphate dihydrate (DCPD) were detected in samples prepared with soaking times of 110 s (110 s, 5 c, and 110 s, 15 c).

FT-IR spectra of pGelMA plane models after ASP at conditions of 10 s, 5 c (a); 10 s, 15 c (b); 110 s, 5 c (c); and 110 s, 15 c (d), and pGelMA xerogel (e). The asterisks indicate peaks assignable to bending vibrations (nu4, 650-500 cm-1) of PO43-.

XRD diffraction patterns of pGelMA plane models after ASP at conditions of 10 s, 5 c (a); 10 s, 15 c (b); 110 s, 5 c (c); and 110 s, 15 c (d), and synthetic HAp (e). The asterisks and circles show peaks corresponding to typical peaks of HAp and DCPD, respectively.

The ratio of the inorganic compounds to the total weight of the GelMA hydrogels after ASP under each condition was evaluated using DTA-TGA. The calculated ratios of the inorganic compounds to the total weight of the GelMA hydrogel plane after ASP were 10.0% (10 s, 5 c), 21.1% (10 s, 15 c), 23.5% (110 s, 5 c), and 28.8% (110 s, 15 c) (Figure 8).
Proportion of inorganic compounds in pGelMA plane models after each ASP condition. Asterisks indicate a significant difference (*p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, Student's t-test).
Culture of MSCs on Composite Scaffolds

The morphology and viability of MSCs cultured on the pGelMA-HAp composite scaffolds were examined by using pGelMA hydrogel discs. ASP was conducted on the pGelMA hydrogel discs (Figure 2f) using the same procedure and conditions as those used for the line and plane models. MSCs seeded on pGelMA hydrogel discs after ASP under the four conditions and cultured for 24 h were stained with calcein AM and EthD-1. On the pGelMA-HAp discs prepared at 10 s, 5 c, most MSCs stained green were highly spread on the discs (Figure 9a). On the discs prepared under the conditions of 10 s, 15 c and 110 s, 5 c, most MSCs also stained green, but the cell spreading was lower and rounded (Figure 9b,c). On the discs prepared at 110 s, 15 c, most of the cells were round in shape, and many cells were stained red (Figure 9d) (cell viability: 10 s, 5 c; 96.4%, 10 s, 15 c; 97.7%, 110 s, 5 c; 91.7%, 110 s, 15 c; 80.5%).
LIVE/DEAD fluorescence images of MSCs cultured on pGelMA hydrogels after ASP at conditions of 10 s, 5 c (a); 10 s, 15 c (b); 110 s, 5 c (c); and 110 s, 15 c (d) for 24 h. Scale bars: 200 mum.
Fabrication of Pyramid Hydrogel Models and Modification with HAp

A 3D model with a pyramidal structure composed of three layers (Figure 1b-d) was designed and fabricated (Figure 10a). ASP with a condition of 10 s, 5 c was conducted on the fabricated pyramid model to modify it with HAp. After ASP, the pyramid model turned white, but there was not a significant loss of the detailed 3D microstructure (Figure 10b). CLSM images showed that MSCs attached and spread on the different stages of the pyramidal structure such as the middle (Figure 11a,d) and lower (Figure 11c,f), while small cells were observed between them (Figure 11b,e).
Microscopic images of the pyramid model of pGelMA hydrogel before (a) and after (b) ASP at the 10 s, 5 c condition. Scale bars: 500 mum.

CLSM images of MSCs cultured on the pyramid model of the pGelMA hydrogel after ASP (10 s, 5 c). Pyramidal middle stage (a, d), between the middle and lower stages (b, e), and lower stage (c, f). Scale bars: 200 mum (x10; a-c. x 20; d-f).
Discussion

pGelMA hydrogel line models with certain line widths (Table S1) were fabricated by using stereolithography by varying the laser power. The line widths were 100 (Figure S1a-d), 300 (Figure S2a-d), and 600 mum (Figure 3a-d). After ASP, all line models with dimensions of 100, 300, and 600 mum were successfully modified with inorganic components (Figures 3i-l, S1e-h, and S2e-h), and the plate- and needle-like structures characteristic of HAp were observed on the surfaces of the composites in the SEM images (Figure 5). In the case of line models with a 600 mum width after ASP at 10 s, 5 c and 10 s, 15 c, white-colored components stained with alizarin red S were observed near the surface of the models (Figure 3e,f,i,j). Alizarin red S can form a complex with calcium ions; therefore, deposits containing calcium ions can be selectively stained red. For ASP at 110 s, 5 c and 110 s, 15 c, the entire model was uniformly stained (Figure 3k,l). For further investigation, SEM-EDX mappings of cross section were also performed on 600 mum pGelMA line models. From these EDX mappings (Figure 4), two types of deposition patterns were distinguished: near the surface and throughout the model. At an immersion time of 10 s, calcium (red) and phosphorus (blue) were present only near the surface of the models, and uncolored areas were observed in the center of the models (Figure 4b,c,e,f). In contrast, at an immersion time of 110 s, calcium (red) and phosphorus (blue) were detected in all of the models (Figure 4h,i,k,l). These results suggest that neither calcium nor phosphate ions penetrated very deeply into the models after ASP with a shorter immersion time of 10 s and that deposits formed only near the surface of the line models. After ASP at a longer immersion time of 110 s, calcium and phosphorus penetrated the center of the line models. Hence, the results obtained from EDX mapping, in combination with the alizarin red S staining, can demonstrate the locations of deposit formation. It has been reported that the HAp layer after ASP was increased by increasing the immersion time during the modification of the polymer surface, suggesting that the calcium and phosphate ions in the ASP solution penetrated the center of the hydrogel model.

The fact that the entire 100 and 300 mum sized models were fully stained with alizarin red S after all ASP conditions suggests that the ions in the ASP solution moved a distance of 150 mum from the surface of the model, which was half the model line width. This corresponds to the thickness of the deposited layer on the 600 mum pGelMA line models. The sharp peaks of the phosphate groups detected in the FT-IR spectra (Figure 6) indicate the presence of inorganic modifications containing phosphate groups in the samples prepared under all ASP conditions. The XRD results showed that typical peaks of HAp were detected (Figure 7), and the crystallinity of deposits after ASP at 110 s and 15 c (Figure 7d) was higher than those of the other conditions. The XRD peaks at approximately 11 and 21  were sharper at 110 s, 5 c and 110 s, 15 c. These peaks indicated the presence of calcium phosphate dihydrate (DCPD) crystals. By comparing the XRD peaks of commercially available synthetic hydroxyapatite as standard HAp (Figure 7e) with the formed HAp on pGelMA hydrogels after ASP, all data showed typical peaks of HAp, such as (002) at 26 , (211), (112), and (300) at 32 , and (213) at 49 . The XRD peaks of the synthetic HAp were sharper than the peaks of HAp formed after ASP, indicating that the synthetic HAp showed higher crystallinity than HAp from ASP. It has been reported that bone-like HAp has low crystallinity, suggesting that HAp from ASP would be bone-like HAp. In HAp modification on gelatin substrates using ASP, the formation of DCPD as a byproduct has been previously reported. From the report, H+ ions generated during HAp formation had an effect on decreasing pH and promoting DCPD formation. The formation of DCPD in the ASP with an immersion time of 110 s may be attributed to the decrease of pH in the pGelMA hydrogel caused by H+ ion diffusion with a longer immersion time. The structures of DCPD observed large plate-like crystals were not seen from SEM images of pGelMA line models after ASP in each condition. It has been reported that the XRD diffraction pattern corresponding with DCPD was detected, even if the structure of DCPD was not observed from the SEM image. Since DCPD has been reported to be generated because of poor diffusion of H+ ions during HAp formation, to prove the generation of DCPD after ASP, we investigated whether DCPD after ASP was observed on gel discs (width: ca. 1 mm) whose widths were thicker than fabricated pGelMA plane or line models (width: ca. 100-600 mum). As a result, a relatively large amount of DCPD was observed in ASP conditions at 110 s, 5 c and 110 s, 15 c (Figure S3c,d), while DCPD was not observed in ASP conditions at 10, 5 c and 10 s, 15 c (Figure S3a,b). Therefore, DCPD was generated as a byproduct after ASP for a longer immersion time such as 110 s. Raman spectra (Figure S4) also showed that the deposits contained phosphate because peaks were detected that were derived from the P-O stretching vibration, P-O transformation vibration, and P-O unpaired vibration at 960, 400, 600, and 1000 cm-1.

From the DTA-TGA analysis, the thermal behaviors of the organic-inorganic composites were also evaluated. As shown in the TGA curves in Figure S5, endothermic peaks corresponding to dehydration were detected at temperatures of up to 100  C in all samples. Above 200  C, some exothermic peaks could be seen. The first exothermic peak was found at ca. 300  C, indicating a pyrolysis process occurred in the microstructure of the gel component, mainly due to cleavage of the hydrogen bonds between molecules and breakdown of molecular side chains. Exothermic peaks at ca. 500  C have been reported to correspond to the decomposition of gelatin combined with HAp nanocrystals. Therefore, from the TGA curves, which exhibited a gradual decrease in the weight of the organic-inorganic composites (Figure S5), the water, organic, and inorganic fractions in the composites were determined from the regions of the TGA curve measured from the initial temperature (ca. 25  C) to 100  C, 100-600  C, and above 600  C, respectively. When the obtained mineral compositions were compared (Figure 8), the ratio of inorganic deposits after ASP at 10 s and 5 c under mild conditions in this study was lower at 10.0%, and the ratio was higher at 28.8% after ASP at 110 s and 15 c than for the other ASP conditions. At 10 s, 15 c and 110 s, 5 c, there was a similar ratio of inorganic deposits, suggesting that increasing both the immersion time and number of cycles in ASP also helped to form large amounts of HAp. By comparing the result of the DTA curve after ASP at 10 s, 5 c (Figure S5a) with the other three ASP conditions (Figure S5b-d), the intensity of the peak detected at 560-570  C from ASP at 10 s, 5 c was significantly higher than that of the other ASP conditions. When the number of cycles was increased from 5 (10 s, 5 c) to 15 (10 s, 15 c), the intensity of the DTA value decreased. When the immersion time was increased from 10 (10 s, 5 c) to 110 s (110 s, 5 c), the same tendency was observed. For ASP at 110 s and 15 c, the intensity of the peak significantly decreased. These intensities depend on the stability of the pGelMA network after ASP. After ASP at 110 s and 15 c, the network of the pGelMA hydrogel was disturbed by HAp. In addition, by comparing the DTA curve from 10 s, 5 c with the other ASP conditions, intense DTA peaks were shifted higher by about 5  C. These results indicate that GelMA may interact with HAp crystals in organic-inorganic composites after ASP at 10 s, 15 c; 110 s, 5 c; and 110 s, 15 c.

For 10 and 5 c, cell adhesion and cell spreading were observed, whereas for 10 s, 15 c and 110 s and 5 c, some cells were round in shape and did not show cytotoxicity (Figure 9). In contrast, most cells became round and more dead cells were observed. The scaffolds obtained with longer immersion times and a higher number of cycles at 110 s and 15 c showed a clear increase in HAp crystallinity. It is known that cell adhesion is poor on highly crystalline HAp. It is likely that more dead cells were observed under these conditions because cell death of nonadherent cells occurred. This is consistent with the observation that dead cells were present on the composite following ASP of 110 s and 15 c. To evaluate cell growth on pGelMA-HAp composites, an MTT assay was performed. Results showed that the number of cells on composites after ASP at 10 s, 5 c, 10 s, 15 c, and 110 s, 5 c increased up to 72 h, but for 110 s, 15 c (Figure S6). MSCs increased the most on the hydrogels after ASP (10 s and 5 c), suggesting that cell attachment to the surface may promote cell proliferation. The surface with cells on the pGelMA-HAp hydrogel disc after ASP (10 s, 5 c) and its back surface without cells were observed (Figure S7). Results showed that cells were attached to the surface HAp deposits on the hydrogel (Figure S7a) and the HAp deposits were not significantly changed by comparing the back surface without cells (Figure S7b). Therefore, the formed HAp deposits on the pGelMA hydrogel remained after cell culture. The CLSM image also showed that extended MSCs were observed on the pGelMA-HAp composite. From the cross-sectional view of the CLSM image (Figure S8), a ca. 10 mum thick cell layer was observed near the surface of the composite. Considering that the thickness of the single cell is a few microns, it was suggested that the infiltration would not occur.

passages.text: Based on the results obtained in this study, an ASP of 10 s and 5 c produced the best conditions for HAp modification of the fabricated models without significantly changing the fine structure of the models. As a preliminary demonstration of the fine HAp modifications, ASP was performed using a pyramid model. A pyramid model after ASP at 10 s and 5 c was successfully modified with HAp with little structural changes, suggesting that HAp formed only near the surface of the model. HAp modification of bulk hydrogels from ASP was conducted and thick HAp layers with several micrometers were observed near the surface of the hydrogels. This modification technique of HAp in ASP at the condition optimized in this study allows the modification of the thin layer of HAp to hydrogel and even microfabricated 3D models without significant structural changes. And MSCs were attached and spread on the different stages of HAp-modified pyramid models (Figure 11), demonstrating that cells can be seeded on the designed models after HAp modification.

In this study, microsized pGelMA hydrogel models were fabricated, and the mechanism of HAp formation was elucidated. The amount and crystallinity of the formed HAp were changed by varying the immersion time and number of cycles. To construct artificial bone models with porous structures that mimic the structure of natural bone, HAp models with complex 3D structures are required and the construction of a fine structure by pressing or extrusion using HAp powder is difficult. This two-step fabrication method of first fabricating frameworks of hydrogel models by stereolithography and subsequently modifying the fabricated models with HAp allows the creation of fabricated models whose surface is completely modified with HAp and development of 3D cell scaffolds, such as artificial bone marrow with more precise structures.
Conclusions

In this study, we demonstrated that it was possible to modify fine 3D hydrogel models fabricated by stereolithography with HAp. It was also shown that the thickness of the formed HAp layer and the penetration depth of calcium and phosphate ions into the hydrogel models can be controlled by changing ASP conditions. Until now, ASP to bulk hydrogels has been conducted, but this study is the first demonstration of HAp modification to 3D printed models with a more complex structure by ASP. This technique can be achieved with 3D cell culture systems, which differ from the usual two-dimensional cell culture systems using HAp-modified hydrogels. In addition, it will also lead to the development of scaffolds to support bone grafts or to create biological niches, such as artificial bone marrow.

passages.text: Mass Spectrometric Analysis of the Active Site Tryptic Peptide of Recombinant O6-Methylguanine-DNA Methyltransferase Following Incubation with Human Colorectal DNA Reveals the Presence of an O6-Alkylguanine Adductome

Human exposure to DNA alkylating agents is poorly characterized, partly because only a limited range of specific alkyl DNA adducts have been quantified. The human DNA repair protein, O6-methylguanine O6-methyltransferase (MGMT), irreversibly transfers the alkyl group from DNA O6-alkylguanines (O6-alkGs) to an acceptor cysteine, allowing the simultaneous detection of multiple O6-alkG modifications in DNA by mass spectrometric analysis of the MGMT active site peptide (ASP). Recombinant MGMT was incubated with oligodeoxyribonucleotides (ODNs) containing different O6-alkGs, Temozolomide-methylated calf thymus DNA (Me-CT-DNA), or human colorectal DNA of known O6-MethylG (O6-MeG) levels. It was digested with trypsin, and ASPs were detected and quantified by matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization-time-of-flight mass spectrometry. ASPs containing S-methyl, S-ethyl, S-propyl, S-hydroxyethyl, S-carboxymethyl, S-benzyl, and S-pyridyloxobutyl cysteine groups were detected by incubating MGMT with ODNs containing the corresponding O6-alkGs. The LOQ of ASPs containing S-methylcysteine detected after MGMT incubation with Me-CT-DNA was <0.05 pmol O6-MeG per mg CT-DNA. Incubation of MGMT with human colorectal DNA produced ASPs containing S-methylcysteine at levels that correlated with those of O6-MeG determined previously by HPLC-radioimmunoassay (r2 = 0.74; p = 0.014). O6-CMG, a putative O6-hydroxyethylG adduct, and other potential unidentified MGMT substrates were also detected in human DNA samples. This novel approach to the identification and quantitation of O6-alkGs in human DNA has revealed the existence of a human DNA alkyl adductome that remains to be fully characterized. The methodology establishes a platform for characterizing the human DNA O6-alkG adductome and, given the mutagenic potential of O6-alkGs, can provide mechanistic information about cancer pathogenesis.
Introduction

Alkylating agents (AAs) are known human mutagens and carcinogens whose effects are largely mediated by the formation of alkyl adducts in DNA.- The mutational landscape observed in patients with malignant melanomas and glioblastoma multiformes following treatment with the chemotherapeutic methylating agent, Temozolomide, consists primarily of G-A transitions attributed to the generation of O6-methylguanine (O6-MeG) in DNA. A similar mutational signature has recently been described in colorectal cancer implicating AA exposure as a causal factor in this disease.O6-MeG and other O6-alkylguanine (O6-alkG) adducts are repaired by the DNA repair protein, O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT), which provides protection against the toxic, mutagenic, and carcinogenic effects of AA exposure. Increased methylation of CpG islands in the MGMT promoter region has been described in human tumors and is associated with G-A transitions in colorectal, lung, and brain tumors and the Temozolomide-induced mutational signature. Furthermore, MGMT promoter methylation improves overall survival in glioblastoma patients treated with Temozolomide. As promoter methylation downregulates MGMT expression, these results are entirely consistent with persistence of O6-alkGs in DNA as a cause of toxicity and mutational events and provide compelling evidence that AAs are involved in the etiology of some cancers.

passages.text: In addition to this indirect evidence for the presence of O6-alkGs in human DNA, there is increasing direct evidence for their presence in human DNA as described in several reviews- of alkyl DNA adductomes. Thus, O6-MeG,O6-ethyl (O6-EtG),O6-propyl (O6-PrG),O6-butyl (O6-BuG), and O6-carboxymethyl (O6-CMG) as well as 7-alkylguanines and methyl DNA phosphate adducts have all been detected in human DNA. The presence of a wider spectrum of alkyl adducts is not surprising given the wide range of AAs present in the human environment and that AAs can also be generated endogenously from the many varied and abundant dietary and luminal amines and other substrates. These processes likely result in AA exposure that significantly increases mutational and cancer risk by the formation of a range of associated O6-alkGs. Previous studies have largely focused on quantifying the presence of O6-MeG in human DNA using radioimmunoassays (RIA),32P-postlabeling, and mass spectrometry (MS), e.g., high-resolution gas chromatography-MS with selected ion recording and ultrahigh-performance liquid chromatography-high resolution MS/MS, approaches with differing sensitivities and specificities. Some caution may be needed in some cases, for example, antibodies may recognize a range of O6-alkGs and hence the levels of O6-MeG may be overestimated if the O6-MeG is not completely separated from other possible O6-alkGs before the immunoassay quantitation. MS, in particular, has been routinely used in clinical settings and is increasingly used to detect with high sensitivity and specificity a wide range of different DNA adducts using relatively simple procedures that do not need radioactive materials or antibodies.-

In the present paper, we describe a novel method to assess the O6-alkG adductome by the MS analysis of alkylated MGMT active site peptides (ASPs) following in vitro incubation of MGMT with extracted DNA, which results in the irreversible transfer of the alkyl group from the O6 position of the modified guanine bases to the active site cysteine residue in MGMT.
Materials and Methods
Samples

A cross-sectional study of patients presenting with colorectal carcinoma at hospitals within Greater Manchester, U.K., was undertaken. Patients were included if they were undergoing surgery for treatment, and human colorectal tumor (n = 10; obtained from colorectal carcinoma tissue) and macroscopically normal (n = 3; taken ~5 cm from the tumor edge) tissues were obtained from individuals (six men, two women, and two participants of unknown sex). The age of the eight individuals was 69 +- 14 (mean +- SD). DNA was extracted by a phenol/chloroform procedure and analyzed for O6-MeG by an HPLC-radioimmunoassay (RIA) using a [3H]-O6-methyldeoxyguanosine tracer and mouse monoclonal alpha-O6-MedG following Aminex chromatography, and the remaining DNA was stored at -80  C until it was analyzed in the present study. Ethical approval was obtained from East Midlands-Derby Research Ethics Committee, Health Research Authority, NHS (REC reference: 15/EM/0505).
Materials

Synthetic methylated (GNPVPILIPMe-CHR) MGMT-ASP and light and heavy isotope (13C15N proline)-labeled methylated MGMT-ASP corresponding to positions 136-147 of MGMT were purchased from Cambridge Research Biochemicals, Cleveland, U.K. Other chemicals used in this work were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (Poole, Dorset, U.K.) unless otherwise stated. Calf thymus (CT) DNAs containing various levels of O6-MeG (0.050, 0.125, 0.250, and 0.50 pmol/mg-CT-DNA) were prepared by incubating Temozolomide with CT-DNA, and levels were determined by a competitive radioisotope-based assay involving preincubation of incrementally increasing amounts of the Temozolomide-methylated CT DNA with a fixed amount of MGMT and then post incubation with excess N-[3H]methyl-N-nitrosourea (Hartmann Radiochemicals: specific radioactivity 80 Ci/mmole) methylated CT DNA. The decrease in the amount of radioactivity transferred to the MGMT was used to determine the amount of O6-MeG in the Temozolomide-methylated DNA, as described previously.
Expression and Purification of MGMT

Human MGMT was expressed as a maltose-binding protein (MBP) fusion protein from pMAL-2c expression vector constructs and affinity-purified using amylose resin (New England Biolabs Inc., USA) essentially as described previously. For some studies, the MBP-MGMT fusion protein was cleaved with factor Xa, and MGMT was purified using DEAE-sepharose ion exchange chromatography. Human MGMT was also expressed as a hexahistidine (His) fusion protein from pQE30Xa (Qiagen) and purified by nickel affinity chromatography using a complete His-Tag purification resin (Sigma-Aldrich). MGMT activity was subsequently assayed by measuring the transfer of [3H] from N-[3H]-methyl-N-nitrosourea (Hartmann, Germany; specific activity 80 Ci/mmol) methylated CT-DNA to the MGMT fusion protein. In addition, for the Vion IMS QToF analysis, MGMT was synthesized by GeneArt (ThermoFisher), cloned into pNic28-Bsa4 linearized with BsaI-HF (NEB) using In-Fusion ligation independent cloning. Competent BL21(DE3) cells (NEB) were transformed with the vector, His-MGMT expressed, and purified by nickel affinity chromatography.
Synthesis of Oligodeoxyribonucleotides Containing a Single O6-alkG Adduct

O6-alkG-containing 12- or 23 mer-oligodeoxyribonucleotides (ODNs) that contained a single O6-alkG adduct in the following sequences, 5' -SIMA-GCC ATG XCT AGTA or 5'-GAA CTY CAG CTC CGT GCT GGC CC-3', were synthesized as described.- X was unmodified G, O6-MeG, O6-EtG, O6-PrG, O6-hydroxyethyl (O6-HOEtG), O6-benzylG (O6-BnG), O6-pyridyl-oxobutylG (O6-pobG), 2,6-diaminopurine, O6-aminoethylG, N6-hydroxypropyl-2,6-diaminopurine, or O6-methyladamantylG, and Y was unmodified G or O6-MeG or O6-CMG. Modified 12-mer ODNs were characterized by ESI-MS as previously described for the 12-mers and 23-mers in Figure s1.

Control ODNs (with unmodified G bases) as well as complementary ODNs were synthesized by Sigma-Aldrich, U.K. Single-stranded ODNs were annealed to equimolar amounts of the ODN complement by heating to 95  C in 50 mM NaCl for 20 min and then cooling slowly to room temperature for >1 h. ODNs were stored at -20  C.
Preparation of MGMT Tryptic Peptides following Incubation of MGMT with ODNs and Methylated CT-DNA

In a typical assay, double-stranded 23-mer ODNs (20 pmol) containing G, O6-MeG, or O6-CMG or Temozolomide-methylated CT DNA (Me-CT-DNA) were incubated with MBP-MGMT (2 pmol by activity) for 6 h at 37  C in IBSA buffer (1 mg/mL BSA in 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.3 containing 1 mM EDTA and 1 mM Tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine hydrochloride (TCEP)). Trypsin (ratio of MBP-MGMT:trypsin, 20:1) was added, the sample was incubated overnight (18 h) at 37  C with shaking, and then 1% formic acid was added to give a final concentration of 0.1%. MGMT tryptic peptides were desalted, concentrated using Millipore C18-Ziptips (Merck Millipore, Ireland) according to manufacturer's instructions, and eluted in 5 muL of 0.1% formic acid in 50% acetonitrile/water.
Preparation of MGMT Tryptic Peptides following Incubation of MGMT with Human DNA

His-MGMT (30 pmol by activity) was incubated with 2 mg of human colorectal DNA for 6 h at 37  C in 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.3 containing 1 mM EDTA and 2 mM TCEP on a shaker incubator. Prewashed Ni-coated magnetic beads (PureProteome Magnetic Beads, Merck Millipore, U.K.) were resuspended in equilibration buffer, vortex-mixed, added to the His-MGMT/DNA solution, and incubated at 4  C overnight on a rotor mixer (Blood Tube Rotator, SB1, Stuart Scientific, U.K.). The sample was then centrifuged (Fisher Scientific accuSpin Microcentrifuges), and the supernatant was aspirated. Beads were resuspended in 40 muL of buffer containing 50 mM sodium phosphate, 300 mM sodium chloride, and 300 mM imidazole, pH 8. Trypsin was added (as above), and the sample was incubated overnight (18 h) at 37  C with shaking. Formic acid (1%) was added to give a final concentration of 0.1%, and the tryptic peptides were desalted and concentrated using Millipore C18-Ziptips and then spiked with 250 fmol of 13C15N proline-labeled methylated ASP internal standard.
MALDI-ToF MS Analysis of MGMT Active Site Peptides and Data Acquisition

Tryptic peptides arising from MGMT, MBP-MGMT, and His-MGMT were spotted on a MALDI plate together with a saturated alpha-cyano-4-hydroxycinnamic acid (Fluka, Buchs, Switzerland) matrix solution (10 mg/mL in 50% ethanol/acetonitrile). The MALDI-ToF was calibrated by using a J67722 MALDI certified mass spec calibration standard (Alfa Aesar, U.K.). Spectra were acquired over the mass to charge ratio (m/z) range 800-2300 using a Bruker (Germany) Ultraflex II operating at 30% laser intensity and 1000 laser shots per spectrum in reflectron positive ion mode. A signal/noise >10 was required for identification of detected alkylated peptide ions. Peak areas (PAs) of chosen peptides (methylated MGMT-ASP and internal standard) were measured using FlexAnalysis software (Bruker, Germany). Label-free quantitation of O6-CMG adducts was carried out by comparing the PA of carboxymethylated ASP to that of methylated ASP generated from known amounts of the appropriate O6-alkG-containing ODNs and applying this ratio to the PAs of carboxymethylated ASPs found after incubating MGMT with colorectal DNA.
Vion IMS QTof Analysis and Data Acquisition of His-MGMT Active Site Peptides

Control (G) and O6-MeG-containing single-stranded 23-mer ODNs (O6-MeG) (37.5 nmol) were incubated with 50 pmol of His-MGMT in 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.3 containing 1 mM EDTA and 5 mM DTT for 90 min at 37  C. In-solution digestion was performed on the samples with 50 mM DTT, 14 mM iodoacetamide, and trypsin (ratio of His-MGMT:trypsin <= 12:1) was added and incubated overnight (18 h) at 37  C. After in-solution trypsin digestion and concentration, one sample of the single-stranded control ODN (G) was spiked with 112 nmol of synthetic methylated ASP. The samples were dried using an SP Genevac miVac Sample Concentrator and then dissolved in water containing 0.05% acetonitrile and 0.1% formic acid.

Tryptic peptides were resolved by ultraperformance liquid chromatography using an ACQUITY UPLC I-Class System and a 100 x 2.1 mm Hypersil GOLD C18 3 mum column (ThermoFisher) in tandem with a quadruple time-of-flight mass spectrometer (Vion IMS QToF, Waters). Water containing 0.1% formic acid was used as mobile phase A, and acetonitrile containing 0.1% formic acid was used as mobile phase B. The flow rate was 0.2 mL/min, and the total elution time was 60 min. The elution gradient program was as follows: 0 to 3 min, 99% A; 3 to 53 min, 99 to 80% A; 53 to 55 min, 80 to 20% A; 55 to 57 min, 20% A; 57 to 58 min, 20 to 99% A; 58 to 60 min, 99% A. Electrospray ionization was carried out in positive ion mode with an ion source temperature of 120  C. The mass scan range was from 105 to 2000 m/z, with a scan time of 0.250 s. LockSpray solution containing the peptide leucine/enkephalin was analyzed every 2 min to adjust mass calibration of the instrument during analysis. Data were collected in MSE mode where the instrument alternated between low (6 eV for precursor ion collection) and high (15-40 eV ramp for fragment ion collection) collision energies throughout the entire chromatographic run. Data were analyzed using UNIFI software version 1.9.4.053 (Waters Corporation); the selected amino acid modifiers were methyl (cysteine), carbamidomethyl (cysteine), oxidation (methionine), and deamidation (asparagine).
Results
MS Analysis of MGMT Active Site Tryptic Peptides following Incubation of MGMT with O6-alkG-Containing ODNs

Qualitative MS analysis of tryptic fragments of MBP-MGMT following incubation with O6-MeG- and O6-CMG-containing DS ODNs confirmed the transfer of the methyl and carboxymethyl groups from O6-MeG and O6-CMG, respectively, to MGMT: modified MGMT-ASPs were detected by the ions formed from methylated MGMT-ASP (m/z 1329.7 [M + H]+) and carboxymethylated MGMT-ASP (m/z 1373.7 [M + H]+) (Figure 1A,B, respectively). In addition, MS analysis of tryptic digests of MBP-MGMT incubated with DS control G ODNs generated multiple MGMT and MBP peptides and, as expected, only the nonalkylated MGMT-ASP (m/z 1315.73 [M + H]+), as shown in Figure 1C. Ethyl, propyl, benzyl, pyridyloxobutyl, and hydroxyethyl groups were also transferred to the active site cysteine of MGMT from ODNs containing O6-EtG, O6-PrG, O6-BnG, O6-pobG, and O6-HOEtG, respectively (Figure s2 panel A). In contrast, incubation of MGMT with ODNs containing damage not known to be repaired by MGMT such as N6-hydroxypropyl-2,6-diaminopurine, O6-aminoethylG, O6-methyladamantylG, or 2,6-diaminopurine confirmed as expected the lack of transfer of the corresponding alkyl group to MGMT (Figure s2 panel B).

Peak intensities are shown in arbitrary units on the y-axis, and the intensity scale is the same for all panels. The tryptic peptides detected included unmodified MGMT-ASP (GNPVPILIPCHR, 136-147) m/z 1315.73, methylated MGMT-ASP (GNPVPILIP(Me-C)HR, 136-147) m/z 329.74, and carboxymethylated MGMT-ASP (GNPVPILIP(CM-C)HR, 136-147) m/z 1373.73. The peak at m/z 1336.544 is an MBP peptide (SYEEELAKDPR, 332-342).

The presence of methylcysteine in the MGMT ASP was further confirmed after incubation of O6-MeG-containing SS ODNs with His-MGMT, with high confidence detection and identification of the methylated ASP by the fragments obtained with MSE. The ASP was identified as a high confidence peptide with a mass error <2.8 ppm and via tandem mass spectrometry (Table s1, Figures s3-s6).

We then investigated the detection limit of the MALDI-ToF MS assay by using serial dilutions of a synthesized methylated ASP. Linear correlations (amount vs peak area) with R2 values of 0.9985 and 0.9998 were obtained for unlabeled methylated and heavy isotope (13C15N proline)-labeled methylated MGMT-ASP standards, respectively (Figure s7). The lower limit of quantification of unlabeled (m/z = 1329.74) and 13C15N proline-labeled (m/z = 1335.74) methylated MGMT-ASP was found to be <20 fmol with a signal/noise ratio of >16.
MALDI-ToF MS Analysis of MGMT Active Site Peptides following Incubation of MGMT with Methylated CT-DNA

Following His-MGMT incubation with methylated CT-DNA, MALDI-ToF MS analysis of tryptic peptides demonstrated the presence of methylated MGMT-ASP (GNPVPILIPMe-CHR, amino acid residues 136-147) in MGMT tryptic peptides. Figure s7A shows the region of the mass spectra of his-MGMT incubated with methylated CT-DNA (containing 0.125, 0.25, 0.5 pmol of O6-MeG/mg methylated CT-DNA) showing both unmodified and methylated MGMT-ASP ions at m/z 1315.72 and 1329.74, respectively. The observed PAs of methylated MGMT-ASP showed a linear correlation with levels of O6-MeG adducts (Figure s7B), and the LLOQ for MGMT-based detection of O6-MeG in methylated CT-DNA was <0.05 pmol O6-MeG per mg CT-DNA. The optimized approach was verified by considering the recovery of methylated MGMT-ASP following His-MGMT incubation with methylated CT-DNA using the 13C15N internal standard. Based on the ratio of PA-methylated ASP to PA Me-ASP STD recovery values of methylated MGMT-ASP fragments were 39.8 +- 0.9%, 41 +- 3.6%, and 48 +- 7.5% (mean +- SD; n = 3) following His-MGMT incubation with methylated CT-DNA that contained 100, 200, and 400 fmol of O6-MeG, respectively.
Identification of O6-alkylG Adducts in Human Colorectal DNA

Both methylated and carboxymethylated MGMT-ASPs were detected following the incubation of his-MGMT with colorectal DNA. Figure 2 shows the mass spectra for His-MGMT incubated with two different human colorectal tumor DNA samples (96T and 25T) or with unmodified CT-DNA. Both methylated and carboxymethylated MGMT ASPs (m/z 1329.74 [M + H]+ and m/z 1373.73 [M + H]+, respectively) were detected in these two samples, indicating the presence of the respective adducts in both DNA samples.

His-MGMT (50 pmol) was incubated with 2 mg of human colorectal DNA samples (A) 96T, (B) 25T, or (C) unmodified CT-DNA. Peak intensities are shown in arbitrary units on the y-axis, and the intensity scale is the same for all panels. S/N > 10 for all detected alkylated MGMT ASPs. The tryptic peptides (residues 136-147) identified were (i) unmodified MGMT-ASP (GNPVPILIPCHR; m/z 1315.73), (ii) methylated MGMT-ASP (GNPVPILIPMe-CHR; m/z 1329.74), and (iii) carboxymethylated MGMT-ASP (GNPVPILIPCM-CHR; m/z 1373.73).
Quantification of O6-alkylG Adducts in Human Colorectal DNA

Following identification of O6-alkG adducts present in human colorectal DNA samples, MGMT tryptic digests were spiked with 13C15N proline-labeled methylated MGMT-ASP and O6-MeG was quantified. O6-MeG was present in all human colorectal DNA samples analyzed at concentrations that ranged from 6.7 to 11.1 and from 5.1 to 78.2 nmol O6-MeG/mol dG for normal and tumor DNA, respectively (Table 1). For the two patients for which we had paired normal and tumor DNA, the levels of O6-MeG in the tumor DNA were higher. Table 1 also shows the concentrations of O6-MeG adducts in the same human colorectal DNA samples quantified previously using an HPLC-RIA: there was a significant correlation between the results of the two assays, r = 0.86 (p = 0.014).

The levels of O6-CMG in human colorectal tumor DNA ranged from 5.2 to 68.2 nmol of O6-CMG/mol of dG (Table 1). There was no association between O6-MeG and O6-CMG levels in human colorectal DNA (P = 0.93), and the O6-CMG/O6-MeG ratio ranged from 0.44 to 3.30.
Evidence for a Human O6-alkG Adductome

In addition to methylated and carboxymethylated ASPs, a number of other ASPs were detected at varying frequencies following incubation of MGMT with paired colorectal normal and tumor DNA samples (Figure 3). These included ASPs with m/z values of 1459.7, 1461.7, 1477.7, 1530.7, 1546.7, and 1555.7, which correspond to alkyl group modifications of mass between 144 and 240. These modifications have not yet been identified, but, in one sample, a peptide with an m/z of 1359.7 was detected and we hypothesized that this ASP was the result of the transfer of the hydroxyethyl (HOEt) group from O6-hydroxyethyl guanine in the DNA. In support of this, when a synthetic DS ODN containing O6-HOEtG was incubated with MGMT, an ASP ion with the same m/z value was detected (data not shown).

These included unidentified (U) ASPs with m/z values of 1459.7 (labeled U2) found in four samples, 1461.7 (labeled U3) in one sample, 1477.7 (labeled U4) in two samples, 1530.7 (labeled U5) in two samples, 1546.7 (labeled U6) in three samples, and 1555.7 (labeled U7) in four samples.
Discussion

In the present work, we have used MGMT to irreversibly transfer alkyl groups from O6-alkGs in DNA to the active site cysteine residue of the protein and, following tryptic digestion, detected the resulting alkylated ASPs by MALDI-ToF MS. This method was developed and validated using DS ODNs containing O6-MeG and O6-CMG and was able to detect ASPs at levels as low as 50 fmol. The potential scope of the method was demonstrated by using the ODNs containing other O6-alkGs having widely different alkyl group structures. Further validation came from the analysis of human colorectal DNA, which found levels of O6-MeG that were directly comparable to those found in the same human DNA samples by using HPLC-RIA.

Analysis of CR DNA by this approach revealed the presence of not only O6-MeG and O6-CMG in normal and tumor tissue but also a putative O6-HOEtG and a number of other adducts that are currently unidentified. Previous studies have shown that alkyl adducts are present in human DNA from both normal and tumor tissue. For example, O6-MeG has been detected in DNA from both normal and tumor tissue from the GI tract,O6-CMG has been detected in colon tumor samples, and methyl DNA phosphate adducts have been detected in human lung tumor tissue and adjacent normal tissue. In this study, human DNA samples showed varied patterns in the O6-alkG presence, suggesting that individuals have very different patterns of exposure to the responsible AA and/or different levels of expression of endogenous MGMT perhaps as a result of MGMT methylation in tumors. The source of these AAs is currently unknown, but humans are likely exposed to a plethora of environmental and dietary alkylating agents as well as endogenously formed N-nitroso compounds. These are very likely to generate numerous mutagenic O6-alkG DNA adducts that may result in a complex array of genomic modifications, some or all of which may contribute to colorectal carcinogenesis. It is also clear that determining the levels of a single O6-alkG adduct will significantly underestimate human exposure and likely that with increased sensitivity, the method will detect many more unknown alkyl groups. Nevertheless, these data clearly demonstrate the presence of an alkyl adductome that is yet to be completely characterized. The importance of such an alkyl adductome is confirmed by the identification of an AA mutation signature in CR cancers.

The method that we described has two advantages over other current approaches to measure alkyl DNA adducts. First, O6-alkGs are detected independent of the nature of the alkyl group enabling the detection of unknown O6-alkGs in contrast to, for example, antibody-based methods that can only detect known O6-alkGs. Furthermore, the potential cross-reactivity of O6-alkG-derived antibodies with different adducts is avoided. Analysis of human DNA in this study clearly indicates that multiple O6-alkG adducts can be detected in one sample at the same time. Second, by targeting O6-alkGs, this approach focuses on adducts that are biologically relevant because of their pro-mutagenicity and pro-carcinogenicity, in contrast to other adductomic approaches that detect a wide range of DNA adducts, including some that have little biological significance. The assay, however, depends absolutely on the ability of MGMT to repair O6-alkGs by alkyl transfer to ASP cysteine. The range of MGMT repairable O6-alkGs in DNA remains unknown although a range of different O6-alkGs in DNA are known substrates, though not necessarily repaired at the same rate. Optimization of the repair reaction (e.g., by increasing incubation time and the ratio of MGMT to DNA) may increase the ability of the assay to detect poorly repaired substrates, but interestingly, a modified ASP consistent with the presence of O6-HOEt in DNA was detected, and O6-HOEt is a poor MGMT substrate in ODNs. Further indications of the range of alkyl groups that are MGMT substrates comes from work with pseudosubstrates (O6-alkGs in the form of free guanine bases) whose alkyl group is removed by MGMT. More than 75 pseudosubstrates with alkyl group masses ranging from 40 to 319 Da have been synthesized and have been shown to inhibit MGMT activity potentially as a result of alkyl group transfer though competitive inhibition cannot be ruled out (Margison Pers. commun.) Where this has been assessed, the same pseudosubstrate following its incorporation into an ODN is significantly more potent at MGMT inactivation.O6-alkGs in DNA that are not MGMT substrates, such as O6-methyladamantylG, were not detected by this assay. At present, neither the nature nor the biological significance of MGMT-irreparable O6-alkGs is known, but if they are not repaired by other DNA repair pathways such as nucleotide excision repair and are also mutagenic, they may also be deleterious to cells. However, associations between downregulation of MGMT via promoter methylation and increased GC-AT transition mutations in human DNA and an alkylating agent mutation signature- clearly demonstrate that MGMT substrates are important in human mutagenesis and such adducts would be detected by our methodology.

This current study used MALDI-ToF MS analysis for detection of alkylated MGMT-ASPs, and the evidence of the detection of the alkylated peptides following MGMT incubation with human colorectal DNA was based on the following three criteria: (1) m/z of detected ions, (2) recorded change in the molecular weight of the ASP (observed mass shift), and (3) S/N > 10. This strategy allows accurate and reproducible quantification of O6-alkG adducts in terms of quantifying detected alkylated peptides using isotopically labeled (13C15N) internal standards at low cost. Furthermore, the assay offers the necessary sensitivity that is critical to detect the inherently low level of O6-alkG adducts. Though we do not have tandem MS data to confirm the identity of the putative alkylated peptides detected in MGMT digest following incubation with human DNA, levels of O6-MeG detected by this assay were correlated with those detected by an HPLC-RIA. Furthermore, the ready availability of DNA containing O6-alkG adducts using the methods that we have described previously allows in principle the generation of any alkylated ASP standard following incubation of the DNA with MGMT. In addition, our novel assay analyzed relatively large amounts of human colorectal DNA, which, although it facilitates the detection of low levels of O6-alkG, may not always be available. To overcome the limitation of low DNA amounts, we are currently investigating the use of targeted MS assays that rely on reaction monitoring, e.g., multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) on a tandem quadrupole instrument and/or parallel reaction monitoring (PRM) on the Thermo Orbitrap series.

In summary, our current work, coupling the action of MGMT with MALDI-ToF MS analysis, provides a novel, sensitive approach for the simultaneous detection of overall DNA O6-guanine alkylation damage in human DNA and, where standards are available, allows the level of known individual adducts to be determined. The sensitivity of the method is limited by the amounts of DNA that can be extracted and analyzed, the ability of MGMT to remove the alkyl groups from the O6-alkGs, and the potential for extremely rare adducts that are potential MGMT substrates that might be present at levels that are less than the lowest limit of quantitation. Furthermore, future development of the methodology should enable the identification of previously unknown O6-alkG adducts in human DNA and hence a comprehensive description of the O6-alkG adductome and its potential contribution to the etiology of human cancer.

passages.text: Evolutionary Spread of Distinct O-methyltransferases Guides the Discovery of Unique Isoaspartate-Containing Peptides, Pamtides
Abstract

Ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs) are a structurally diverse class of natural products with a distinct biosynthetic logic, the enzymatic modification of genetically encoded precursor peptides. Although their structural and biosynthetic diversity remains largely underexplored, the identification of novel subclasses with unique structural motifs and biosynthetic pathways is challenging. Here, it is reported that peptide/protein L-aspartyl O-methyltransferases (PAMTs) present in several RiPP subclasses are highly homologous. Importantly, it is discovered that the apparent evolutionary transmission of the PAMT gene to unrelated RiPP subclasses can serve as a basis to identify a novel RiPP subclass. Biochemical and structural analyses suggest that homologous PAMTs convert aspartate to isoaspartate via aspartyl-O-methyl ester and aspartimide intermediates, and often require cyclic or hairpin-like structures for modification. By conducting homology-based bioinformatic analysis of PAMTs, over 2,800 biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) are identified for known RiPP subclasses in which PAMTs install a secondary modification, and over 1,500 BGCs where PAMTs function as a primary modification enzyme, thereby defining a new RiPP subclass, named pamtides. The results suggest that the genome mining of proteins with secondary biosynthetic roles can be an effective strategy for discovering novel biosynthetic pathways of RiPPs through the principle of "guilt by association".

Comprehensive bioinformatic analysis demonstrates the close evolutionary relationship of peptide/protein L-aspartyl O-methyltransferases (PAMTs) found in biosynthetic gene clusters for ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs). Genome mining, heterologous expression, mass analysis, and multidimensional nuclear magnetic resonance analyses uncover pamtides, a unique subclass of RiPPs containing isoaspartyl moiety.
Introduction

Ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs) are a rapidly expanding class of natural products. RiPPs exhibit a unique biosynthetic pathway that involves genetically encoded precursor peptides and enzymes, with the latter installing diverse post-translational modifications (PTMs) on the precursor peptides. The precursor peptides typically have two modules: the leader and core regions, which are recognized and modified by PTM enzymes, respectively. This biosynthetic simplicity and modularity, and thereby high evolvability, underlies not only the structural and functional diversity of RiPPs but also the high potential for engineering novel functional biomolecules.

The hallmark of RiPP diversity is the distinct PTMs and associated biosynthetic pathways, which individually define the subclasses of RiPPs. The number of RiPP subclasses has increased from 23 in 2013 to 41 in 2021, highlighting the recent expansion of the RiPP diversity, which is likely to continue in the near future. Discovery of new RiPP subclasses has traditionally relied on fortuitous isolation by activity-based screening. While the explosion of genome sequence data and development of genome mining tools have allowed the identification of a large number of putative biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) for RiPPs, these methods are generally inefficient at uncovering novel RiPP subclasses; unlike nonribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs), RiPP biosynthetic enzymes lack common features across all RiPP subclasses, and therefore, the typical genome mining approach based on homology of biosynthetic enzymes is mostly limited to the expansion of known or closely related RiPP subclasses.

Dissecting phylogenetically distinct orphan BGCs has proven effective for revealing novel PTMs and RiPP-associated pathways, exemplified by recent discoveries of spliceotides, ranthipeptides, streptides, pearlins, and triceptides. However, this approach depends on the functional divergence of enzymes known for other class-defining PTMs and has particularly been successful with an enzyme family with versatile activities, radical S-adenosylmethionine (rSAM) enzymes. Furthermore, it is often challenging to find candidate BGCs that significantly diverge from those responsible for known PTMs. To bypass the requirement for homologous biosynthetic enzymes, a marker-independent strategy called decRiPPter has recently emerged. This method uncovered a new subfamily of lanthipeptides, but it may be biased on the characteristics of known RiPP precursors and requires further exploration to unveil novel PTMs. Overall, new strategies are needed to systematically uncover the unexplored chemical and biosynthetic space associated with RiPPs.

Here, using homologs of protein L-(iso)aspartyl O-methyltransferases (PIMTs), we demonstrate that the genome mining of a secondary modification enzyme can promote the identification of a novel RiPP subclass. PIMTs, also known as L-isoaspartyl protein carboxyl methyltransferases (PCMs), were originally discovered as repair enzymes for damaged proteins. They catalyze the conversion of isoaspartate (isoAsp), which is spontaneously formed from an Asp or Asn residue, to Asp (Figure  1a). Recently, PIMT homologs were found in BGCs of several RiPP subclasses, including lanthipeptides, lasso peptides, and graspetides, where they install secondary modifications on conserved Asp residues. This results in the formation of an aspartimide or isoAsp, the former of which can be spontaneously hydrolyzed to the latter or Asp (Figure 1).

We have expanded the structural diversity of the graspetide family of RiPPs, also known as omega-ester-containing peptides (OEPs). Graspetides and their biosynthesis have been also studied by bioinformatic, biochemical, and structural analyses. Using heterologous co-expression, in vitro reconstitution of enzyme reactions, and structural analyses of the product peptides with mass spectrometry and nulear magnetic resonance (NMR), we discovered that SsfM, a PIMT homolog associated with graspetide biosynthesis, has the same activity as other PIMT homologs in RiPP biosynthesis. Genome mining of PIMT homologs revealed not only homologous enzymes playing a secondary role for known RiPP subclasses but also those mediating the same conversion of Asp as the primary modification, leading to a new RiPP subclass. This result highlights the potential of leveraging the evolutionary dissemination of tailoring enzymes across diverse RiPP BGCs to identify a novel biosynthetic pathway of RiPPs.
Results and Discussion
O-methyltransferase-Associated Gene Cluster Produces an Isoaspartate-Containing Pentacyclic Graspetide

Previous genome mining studies of graspetides have revealed the high co-occurrence of PIMT homologs in graspetide BGCs (group 13 graspetides). Heterologous expression of genes in two BGCs yielded aspartimidylated graspetides. Here, we tested another graspetide BGC from Streptomyces sp. F-3, encoding a precursor peptide (SsfA), an ATP-grasp enzyme (SsfB), and a PIMT homolog (SsfM; Figure  2a). Heterologous co-expression of SsfA and SsfB in Escherichia coli (E. coli) produced the SsfB-modified SsfA, named SsfA(B), which was 90 Da lighter than SsfA (Figure 2b). Incubation of the GluC-digested SsfA(B), SsfA(B)63-97, with methoxide resulted in up to five-fold methanolysis, suggesting that SsfA(B)63-97 has five ester linkages (Figure S1a, Supporting Information). The tandem mass (MS/MS) analysis of the fivefold methanolized SsfA(B)63-97 suggested that the five ring-forming carboxylates reside within the C-terminal 12 residues, which have only four Asp residues and no Glu (Figure S1b, Supporting Information). This result suggests the involvement of the C-terminal carboxylate in ester formation, generating a side-to-end linkage not previously observed in graspetides. Various efforts to determine the ring connectivity using the previously established tandem mass (MS/MS) analysis of reaction intermediates or partially hydrolyzed products were unsuccessful. Collectively, these data suggest that the PIMT homolog-containing BGC produces a graspetide.
